name: Tomcat Manager Shell Upload
short_description: Upload a malicious WAR file to Tomcat Manager for remote code execution.
description: Apache Tomcat's Manager application allows deploying web apps. If you have valid credentials (often defaults like tomcat/tomcat), you can upload a malicious WAR file that gives you a shell. This is a common attack against misconfigured Java servers.
handler_message:
The Tomcat server at 172.20.0.19 handles Cerberus deployment staging. This is where their operators push code to production systems.

David Chen's notes mentioned 'active builds' on this server. Whatever NIGHTFALL is, pieces of it are being assembled here. Marcus Webb signed off on a deployment three days ago.

The Manager interface uses default credentials. Sloppy, but these internal systems were never meant to be exposed.

Get inside. Find out what they're building. The clock is ticking.
episode_intro:
David Chen knew something. He was building evidence, screenshots, logs. And then he vanished.

His notes pointed here - Cerberus's internal deployment infrastructure. If NIGHTFALL is real, if it's more than paranoid speculation, the proof is on this server.

Your hands are shaking. You haven't slept in thirty hours. The car outside your building moved yesterday, but you don't know where it went.

Focus. One target at a time.
episode_outro:
The build manifests confirm it. NIGHTFALL isn't just real - it's almost ready.

SCADA-BRIDGE. That's what they're calling it. A toolkit designed to compromise industrial control systems. Power grids. Water treatment. Gas pipelines.

The deployment is scheduled for 72 hours from now. And buried in the code comments, you find something worse: Chinese language strings. Mandarin error messages. Beijing IP addresses hardcoded as 'attribution markers.'

They're not just planning an attack. They're planning to frame another country for it.

You need to move faster. The executive file shares might have the authorization chain - who approved this, who funded it, who benefits.

But as you disconnect, a notification flashes in your peripheral vision. A new device just connected to your home network.

They're getting closer.

interstitial.title: Episode 3: THE DEPLOYMENT
interstitial.content:
PREVIOUSLY: You found the first references to NIGHTFALL on a forgotten FTP server. A scheduling document. A list of internal IPs. And a name - David Chen.

David was a senior systems administrator at Cerberus. Twenty years of experience. TS/SCI clearance. He started asking questions about NIGHTFALL three weeks ago.

Then he disappeared.

You accessed his home workstation. His browser history told the story - he was scared, he was gathering evidence, he was trying to figure out who to trust.

He never found out. But you found what he left behind: screenshots of internal memos, and a Tomcat deployment URL.

Whatever Cerberus is building, it's on that server. And you need to get inside.

steps.title: Scan the deployment server
steps.narrative: First rule of engagement: verify your target. Nmap with -sV does service version detection - it doesn't just tell you a port is open, it tells you what's listening. For a Tomcat server, this confirms the version and helps identify potential vulnerabilities. Cerberus runs their deployment pipeline here. Time to see what version they're running.

steps.title: Probe the Manager interface
steps.narrative: Tomcat's Manager application is the control panel for deployments - it's where administrators upload new web applications. The -I flag makes curl show only headers, a quick way to check if an endpoint exists without downloading content. A 401 Unauthorized response is actually good news: the interface exists and is protected by credentials. We just need to find them.

steps.title: Initialize the attack framework
steps.narrative: Metasploit is the industry-standard penetration testing framework. What you're about to do - uploading a malicious WAR file - is the same technique real attackers use. The difference is authorization. You're exposing a conspiracy. They're just trying to profit.

steps.title: Select the Tomcat exploit module
steps.narrative: This exploit automates everything: it creates a WAR (Web Application Archive) containing a payload, uploads it through the Manager interface, triggers it, and catches the resulting shell. Cerberus should have changed the defaults. They didn't. That's the gap you're walking through.

steps.title: Set the target host
steps.narrative: RHOSTS defines the remote host - your target. In a real engagement, this might be a list of IPs. Today it's singular: the Cerberus deployment server. Every keystroke brings you deeper into their infrastructure.

steps.title: Configure the target port
steps.narrative: Tomcat typically runs on 8080, the conventional alternative HTTP port. Corporate firewalls often block standard ports but allow high-numbered ones. It's security through obscurity - and it never works.

steps.title: Enter the username
steps.narrative: The default Tomcat Manager username. David Chen's notes mentioned this would work on internal systems. Cerberus didn't think anyone would ever reach this server. They were wrong.

steps.title: Enter the password
steps.narrative: Default credentials. The most common vulnerability in the world isn't a zero-day exploit - it's laziness. 'tomcat/tomcat' ships with the installation. Millions of servers never change it. Neither did Cerberus.

steps.title: Choose your payload
steps.narrative: A reverse shell means the target connects back to you, bypassing firewalls that block inbound connections. Java/shell_reverse_tcp is reliable on Tomcat - no dependencies, works across platforms. When this triggers, you'll have command execution on the deployment server.

steps.title: Set your callback address
steps.narrative: LHOST is where the shell phones home - your attack box. This IP needs to be reachable from the target. When the payload executes, it opens a connection back to this address. Metasploit will be listening.

steps.title: Execute the exploit
steps.narrative: This is it. Metasploit packages the payload into a WAR file, authenticates to the Manager, uploads it as a 'legitimate' application, deploys it, triggers execution, and catches the callback. In seconds, you're inside Cerberus infrastructure. The deployment server that's building NIGHTFALL.

steps.title: Verify shell access
steps.narrative: Raw reverse shells don't show a prompt - the cursor just blinks. Don't let that fool you. Type 'id' and press Enter. The response tells you who you are on the target system. Root means full control. You're inside.

steps.title: Upgrade to interactive shell
steps.narrative: Raw shells are functional but awkward - no prompt, no command history, Ctrl+C kills your session. Spawning an interactive bash gives you a proper terminal experience. Small quality-of-life improvement that matters during extended reconnaissance.

steps.title: Enumerate system users
steps.narrative: The passwd file lists every user account on the system. Look for service accounts, admin users, anything suggesting multiple operators. Each username is a potential target for lateral movement. Each is someone who might know about NIGHTFALL.

steps.title: Map the network position
steps.narrative: Now you're inside, you need to understand where 'inside' is. The ip addr command shows network interfaces - what networks this server can reach. Internal systems are rarely isolated. This deployment server might have access to production, to databases, to other targets.

steps.title: Discover internal hosts
steps.narrative: Docker environments often expose other containers through the hosts file. These are your next targets. Each internal hostname is another system Cerberus thought was safe. Each is another piece of the NIGHTFALL puzzle.

steps.title: Automated exploitation (bonus)
steps.narrative: Now that you understand the attack chain, the 'pwn' script automates it. Exit your shell (type 'exit' twice) and run this from Kali. Same result, faster execution. Use it for practice or demonstrations. But always understand what's happening under the hood.

success_criteria: You have a root shell on the Cerberus deployment server. You can explore the system, examine build artifacts, and understand what NIGHTFALL actually is.
